index.title: The Vertical Filter on a Cross
index.prompt: A bright row is added through the running example's bright column, so the image becomes a cross, and the same vertical filter is slid over it. Decide which rows of the 4 by 4 feature map change and what they become.
index.answer: Rows 1 to 3 of the map become −2, 4, −2, 0, and row 4 stays −3, 6, −3, 0. Map row i covers image rows i to i + 2, so map rows 1, 2 and 3 take in image row 3 and map row 4, over rows 4 to 6, does not. Over columns 2 to 4, two rows of the window read 0, 1, 0 and give 2 each, and the bright row reads 1, 1, 1 and gives 0, so the total is 4 where it was 6. Over columns 1 to 3 the bright row gives 0 where the line's row gave −1, so −3 becomes −2, and the same over columns 3 to 5. The filter answers a column brighter than its neighbors, and where the bright row crosses its window the neighbors are bright too.

index.title: A Convolution Layer and a Patch Embedding in NumPy
index.prompt: A real convolution layer takes several input channels and several filters, and it has a stride and padding. A Vision Transformer's patch embedding is the same layer with the stride equal to the filter size, computed as one matrix product. Write both in NumPy, in PyTorch's layout: an image is channels x height x width and a stack of filters is output channels x input channels x k x k. The filter is not flipped, so this is what PyTorch's Conv2d computes. 2 parts.
index.answer: Auto-graded inside the notebook. On the chapter's 6 by 6 line image with the two 3 by 3 filters, conv2d must give 2 maps of 4 by 4 with the vertical map -3, 6, -3, 0 in every row and the horizontal map 0 everywhere. On a 2-channel 4 by 5 image with a 3 by 3 filter it must give 4, 5, 6 over 13, 7, -2 at stride 1 with no padding and 8, -3, -2 over 6, 7, -4 at stride 2 with padding 1, and patches on a 2 by 4 by 6 array must give 6 rows of 8 values, one row per patch with channel 0 row by row then channel 1, the rows running along the top row of patches first. patch_embed must agree with conv2d at a stride equal to the patch size.

index.title: Every Column the Line Can Take
index.prompt: A 6 by 6 image holds a single vertical line, and the line could be in any of its six columns. For each column apply the vertical filter, ReLU and 2 by 2 max pooling, add up all 24 pooled values, and say which columns lose the line altogether and what change to the convolution would let the vertical filter find them. 2 parts.
index.answer: Worked solutions are given part by part on the problem page. Attempt each part on paper before revealing it.

theory.title: The Vertical Filter on a Cross

prompt.p: The running example gets a second stroke: row 3 is made bright as well, so the image is a cross. Column 3 and row 3 are 1, and every other pixel is 0.

The vertical filter, with the row −1, 2, −1 three times, slides over it one pixel at a time with no padding, as in the running example. For the line alone, every row of the 4 × 4 feature map was −3, 6, −3, 0. What does the bright row do to that map?

choices.text: Nothing: a full row of 1s under the filter adds −1 + 2 − 1 = 0, so every row of the map stays −3, 6, −3, 0
choices.explain: This treats the bright row as a full row of 1s laid on top of the line. Its pixel in column 3 was already 1 and already counted in the line's total, so the row adds only the pixels on either side of the line. Look at which filter weights those new pixels meet.

choices.text: Rows 1 to 3 of the map become −2, 4, −2, 0, and row 4 stays −3, 6, −3, 0
choices.explain: Map row i covers image rows i to i + 2, so map rows 1, 2 and 3 take in image row 3 and map row 4, over rows 4 to 6, does not. Over columns 2 to 4, two rows of the window read 0, 1, 0 and give 2 each, and the bright row reads 1, 1, 1 and gives 0, so the total is 4 where it was 6. Over columns 1 to 3 the bright row gives 0 where the line's row gave −1, so −3 becomes −2, and the same over columns 3 to 5. The filter answers a column brighter than its neighbors, and where the bright row crosses its window the neighbors are bright too.

choices.text: Only row 3 of the map changes, to −2, 4, −2, 0, and the other rows stay −3, 6, −3, 0
choices.explain: This changes only the map row that sits level with image row 3. A map row is named by the top row of its window, so map row 3 covers image rows 3 to 5. Count every window, from the top row of the map down, that has image row 3 inside it.

choices.text: All four rows of the map become −2, 4, −2, 0, since every row of the map sees part of the cross
choices.explain: This assumes every window sees part of the bright row because every window sees part of the cross. Map row i covers image rows i to i + 2. Check that range for each map row against image row 3.

answer.p: Map row i covers image rows i to i + 2, so map rows 1, 2 and 3 take in image row 3 and map row 4, over rows 4 to 6, does not. Over columns 2 to 4, two rows of the window read 0, 1, 0 and give 2 each, and the bright row reads 1, 1, 1 and gives 0, so the total is 4 where it was 6. Over columns 1 to 3 the bright row gives 0 where the line's row gave −1, so −3 becomes −2, and the same over columns 3 to 5. The filter answers a column brighter than its neighbors, and where the bright row crosses its window the neighbors are bright too.

answer.result: Rows 1 to 3 of the map become −2, 4, −2, 0, and row 4 stays −3, 6, −3, 0

theory.title: Every Column the Line Can Take
overview: The running example's line is in column 3, and moving it to column 2 leaves the pooled vertical map at 6, 0 in each row. The line could be in any of the six columns. For each one, apply the vertical filter (one pixel at a time, no padding), then ReLU, then 2 × 2 max pooling, as in Steps 2 and 3. The vertical filter's three rows are each −1, 2, −1.

prompt.p: Take all six columns together. Each gives a pooled vertical map of 4 numbers, so the six maps hold 24 values between them. What do they add up to?

answer.p: The filter has 4 positions across a row, over image columns 1 to 3, 2 to 4, 3 to 5 and 4 to 6, so its middle column, the one with weight 2, sits over columns 2, 3, 4 and 5. A line under the middle gives 2 per row of the window, 6 in all. A line under either edge gives −1 per row, −3. All rows of the map are equal, so one row tells the whole story:

answer.tex:
\begin{array}{ccccc}
\text{Column of the line} & \text{Row of the map} & \text{After ReLU} & \text{Row of the pooled map} & \text{Pooled total} \\ \hline
1 & \text{−3, 0, 0, 0} & \text{0, 0, 0, 0} & \text{0, 0} & 0 \\
2 & \text{6, −3, 0, 0} & \text{6, 0, 0, 0} & \text{6, 0} & 12 \\
3 & \text{−3, 6, −3, 0} & \text{0, 6, 0, 0} & \text{6, 0} & 12 \\
4 & \text{0, −3, 6, −3} & \text{0, 0, 6, 0} & \text{0, 6} & 12 \\
5 & \text{0, 0, −3, 6} & \text{0, 0, 0, 6} & \text{0, 6} & 12 \\
6 & \text{0, 0, 0, −3} & \text{0, 0, 0, 0} & \text{0, 0} & 0
\end{array}

answer.p: Every row of the map is the same, so each pooled map has two equal rows and its total is twice its row: 0, 12, 12, 12, 12, 0, and 48 over the six columns.

Each of the four middle columns keeps a 6, in columns 2 and 3 in the left block of the map and in columns 4 and 5 in the right one, so the pooled map has two forms, 6, 0 and 0, 6. Pooling absorbs a shift only within a block.

prompt.p: Which columns lose the line altogether, and why? What change to the convolution would let the vertical filter find them?

answer.p: Columns 1 and 6. A line in column 1 is only ever under the left edge of the window, where it meets a weight of −1, so its one response is −3, and ReLU turns that into 0. Column 6 is the same at the right edge. After ReLU nothing is left of the line, and the pooled map is the same as for an empty image.

A border of zeros (padding of 1, as in [Step 2](/module/?id=vision-convolution)) gives the filter 6 positions across, one centered on every column, and the map becomes 6 × 6. A line in column 1 then sits under the middle of the first window and gives 6, or 4 in the top and bottom rows of the map, where the window hangs over the border and covers only two pixels of the line. Sharing one filter across positions finds a pattern everywhere only where the filter can be centered.
